source.title: Normalization Layer Per-Example Gradients are Sufficient to Predict Gradient Noise Scale in Transformers
source.authors: Gavia Gray; Aman Tiwari; Shane Bergsma; Joel Hestness

record.tranche_reason: Appendix C.1 tests a small-scale, fixed-FLOP model-size comparison using validation loss, rather than reproducing the original scaling-law fits.
record.gate_note: The relevant result is the Appendix C.1 comparison of 70M, 111M and 161M models at a constant FLOP budget. The paper's GNS measurements, batch-size schedule, kernel timing, and cited scaling-law results do not test the listed claim versions and are not rows.
record.test_reason: Appendix C.1 runs a small isoFLOP check on a new dataset (OpenWebText). It asks whether the Chinchilla-optimal 111M Cerebras-GPT recipe, tuned on the Pile, is still the loss minimum among 70M, 111M and 161M models at one fixed FLOP budget. This bears on V3 at a single budget only. The rest of the paper (GNS, kernels, batch-size schedule, Flash-attention fix) does not bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude the Cerebras-GPT (Chinchilla-optimal) protocol is optimal within 70M–161M on OpenWebText at this FLOP budget. They assume 111M is good enough, while allowing a better size may lie between 70M and 161M. They also note the learning rate could be increased overall. This is a sanity check supporting the paper's GNS experiments, not a scaling-law study.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Cerebras-GPT training recipes and a small 70M–161M OpenWebText fixed-FLOP comparison; it does not fit or extrapolate the original scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate was varied to locate the loss minimum at each model size.
record.problems: The claim-relevant model-size comparison covers only three sizes at one fixed compute budget. No uncertainty is stated for that comparison, and the figure's annotated minima cannot be reliably assigned to individual sizes from the extracted layout.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant results were reported. GNS and batch-size-scheduling results, kernel performance, and cited results were omitted because they do not measure the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: How the optimal parameter and token counts grow across compute budgets; whether that growth is a stable power law; the Kaplan vs Hoffmann exponents. Only one budget and three sizes were tested, and only hidden size was varied.

record.verdict_notes: The check is incidental to the paper's main contribution (per-example gradient norms and GNS). Treat the support as weak: it shows the Hoffmann-style optimum roughly transfers from the Pile to OpenWebText at roughly 111M scale. It says nothing about the power-law form of the allocation.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law loss relationship across parameters, tokens or compute is measured.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
Tests one fixed-FLOP comparison among three model sizes on OpenWebText, not growth of optimal parameter and token counts across multiple compute budgets or whether either follows a stable power law.
No controlled comparison of depth, width or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime is tested for the claimed power-law form.
No downstream-task performance is measured against scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not fit exponents or compare scaling-law fitting choices; the single-budget comparison cannot establish whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: 70M, 111M and 161M models (aggregate comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation loss across model sizes with token budgets chosen to keep total FLOPs constant; varied learning rate to find the loss minimum at each size.

conditions.value: constant total FLOPs across model sizes
varied to find a minimum at each model scale

rows.baseline: The other two model sizes at the same total FLOP budget
rows.value: The authors state that the 111M model had the lowest loss of the three. Figure 10 annotates minima of 3.246, 3.230 and 3.238, but the text extraction does not unambiguously map each annotation to a model.
rows.note: The authors conclude the training protocol is optimal within the tested range, while noting a better model might lie between 70M and 161M parameters. The numeric minima are reported in the figure but are not assigned to individual model sizes here because the extracted layout does not support that assignment.
rows.check: State holds only for the local claim: the Chinchilla-predicted size is the minimum at one budget. The row cannot show how the optimal size grows with compute. On the value: the stated lowest-loss model is 111M, so the 3.230 annotation (lr 1.17e-03) is most likely 111M. The other two minima (3.246, 3.238) cannot be assigned with confidence. The gaps are about 0.01 nats, from a single seed with no uncertainty, and only three sizes were tested. Token counts per size are not stated.

relationships.condition: OpenWebText, one fixed FLOP budget (Cerebras-GPT 111M recipe), 70M/111M/161M sizes with learning rate swept per size
relationships.reason: At this budget the Chinchilla-optimal 111M model had the lowest validation loss of the three sizes (r1). Margins are small (~0.01), from a single seed, at a single budget.
relationships.display_finding: The 111M model beat the 70M and 161M alternatives in validation loss by margins around 0.01 in a single-seed comparison.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
